title: Adversus Marcionem
author: Tertullian
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0275.stoa006.opp-lat1, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.

passages.original: Ut ergo aliquid et de isto huius mundi indigno loquar, cui et apud Graecos ornamenti et cultus, non sordium nomen est, indignas videlicet substantias ipsi illi sapientiae professores, de quorum ingeniis omnis haeresis animatur, deos pronuntiaverunt, ut Thales aquam, ut Heraclitus ignem, ut Anaximenes aÃ«rem, ut Anaximander universa caelestia, ut Strato caelum et terram, ut Zeno aÃ«rem et aetherem, ut Plato sidera, quod genus deorum igneum appellat, cum de mundo, considerando scilicet et magnitudinem et vim et potestatem et honorem et decorem, opem, fidem, legem singulorum elementorum, quae omnibus gignendis, alendis, conficiendis, reficiendisque conspirant, ut plerique physicorum formidaverint initium ac finem mundo constare, ne substantiae eius, tantae scilicet, minus dei haberentur, quas colunt et Persarum magi et Aegyptiorum hierophantae et Indorum gymnosophistae.
passages.english: So, to say something also about this 'unworthy' thing, this world, which even among the Greeks has the name of ornament and adornment, not of filth: those very professors of wisdom, from whose talents every heresy draws its life, pronounced these 'unworthy' substances to be gods, as Thales [did] water, Heraclitus fire, Anaximenes air, Anaximander all the heavenly bodies, Strato heaven and earth, Zeno air and ether, Plato the stars, which he calls a fiery kind of gods; while concerning the world, considering of course the greatness and force and power and honour and beauty, the help, the reliability, the law of the individual elements, which work together for begetting, nourishing, completing and renewing all things, most of the natural philosophers shrank from [saying] that the world had a beginning and an end, lest its substances, so great as they are, should be held less [than] divine, [substances] which the magi of the Persians and the hierophants of the Egyptians and the gymnosophists of the Indians worship.
passages.notes: 'aÃ«rem' is a mis-encoding of 'aërem' (air). The phrase 'minus dei haberentur' is compressed; rendered 'held less [than] divine'.

passages.original: Erit enim et locus deus, non tantum qua deo maior, sed et qua innatus et infectus ac per hoc aeternus et deo par, in quo semper deus fuerit. Dehinc si et ille mundum ex aliqua materia subiacente molitus est innata et infecta et contemporali deo, quemadmodum de creatore Marcion sentit, redigis et hoc ad maiestatem loci, qui et deum et materiam, duos deos, clusit. Et materia enim deus, secundum formam divinitatis innata scilicet et infecta et aeterna. Aut si de nihilo molitus est mundum, hoc et de creatore sentire cogetur, cui materiam subicit in substantia mundi.
passages.english: For the place too will be a god, not only in that it is greater than god, but also in that it is unborn and unmade and therefore eternal and equal to god, the place in which god has always been. Next, if he too built the world out of some underlying matter, unborn and unmade and contemporaneous with god, as Marcion holds concerning the creator, you reduce this too to the majesty of the place, which has enclosed both god and matter, two gods. For matter too is a god, according to the form of divinity, being of course unborn and unmade and eternal. Or if he built the world out of nothing, [Marcion] will be compelled to hold this also of the creator, to whom he assigns matter as underlying the substance of the world.

passages.original: Huic expeditissimae probationi defensio quoque a nobis necessaria est adversus obstrepitacula diversae partis. Aiunt enim Marcionem non tam innovasse regulam separatione legis et evangelii quam retro adulteratam recurasse. O Christe, patientissime domine, qui tot annis interversionem praedicationis tui sustinuisti, donec scilicet tibi Marcion subveniret!
passages.english: For this most ready proof a defence is also necessary on our part, against the clamourings of the opposing side. For they say that Marcion did not so much innovate the rule [of faith] by his separation of the law and the gospel as restore it after it had been adulterated in the past. O Christ, most patient Lord, who for so many years endured the perversion of your preaching, until, of course, Marcion should come to your rescue!

passages.original: Nunc et de pusillitatibus et malignitatibus ceterisque notis et ipse adversus Marcionem Antitheses aemulas faciam. Si ignoravit deus meus esse alium super se, etiam tuus omnino non scivit esse alium infra se. Quod enim ait Heraclitus ille tenebrosus, eadem via sursum et deorsum'. Denique si non ignorasset, et ab initio ei occurrisset. Delictum et mortem et ipsum auctorem delicti diabolum et omne malum quod deus meus passus est esse, hoc et tuus, qui illum pati passus est.
passages.english: Now I too will make rival Antitheses against Marcion concerning pettinesses and malignities and the other marks [of fault]. If my God did not know that there was another above him, yours too did not know at all that there was another below him. For, as that obscure Heraclitus says, 'the way up and down is the same.' Finally, if he had not been ignorant, he would have confronted him from the beginning. Sin and death and the author of sin himself, the devil, and every evil which my God allowed to exist, this yours also [allowed], who allowed him to allow it.
passages.notes: The logic of the last sentence is compressed; 'pati passus est' plays on 'allow'.

passages.original: Alioquin quam absurdum, ut, si nostrum antiquius probaverimus, Marcionis vero posterius, et nostrum ante videatur falsum quam habuerit de veritate materiam, et Marcionis ante credatur aemulationem a nostro expertum quam et editum, et postremo id verius existimetur quod est serius, post tot ac tanta iam opera atque documenta Christianae religionis saeculo edita, quae edi utique non potuissent sine evangelii veritate, id est ante evangelii veritatem. Quod ergo pertinet ad evangelium interim Lucae, quatenus communio eius inter nos et Marcionem de veritate disceptat, adeo antiquius Marcione est quod est secundum nos, ut et ipse illi Marcion aliquando crediderit, cum et pecuniam in primo calore fidei catholicae ecclesiae contulit, proiectam mox cum ipso, posteaquam in haeresim suam a nostra veritate descivit. Quid nunc, si negaverint Marcionitae primam apud nos fidem eius adversus epistulam quoque ipsius?
passages.english: Otherwise, how absurd [it would be] that, if we prove ours to be older and Marcion's later, ours should seem to be false before it had any material in truth [to falsify], and Marcion's should be believed to have suffered rivalry from ours before it was even published; and finally that that should be thought truer which is later, after so many and such great works and proofs of the Christian religion published to the world, which certainly could not have been published without the truth of the gospel, that is, before the truth of the gospel. So, as concerns for the present the gospel of Luke, in so far as its being shared between us and Marcion is disputed with regard to its truth, the one that is according to us is so much older than Marcion that Marcion himself once believed in it, when also in the first warmth of faith he contributed money to the catholic church, money that was soon thrown out along with himself, after he had defected from our truth into his own heresy. What now, if the Marcionites deny that his first faith was with us, even against his own letter?

passages.original: Denique relictis naviculis secuti sunt eum, ipsum intellegentes qui coeperat facere quod edixerat. Aliud est si affectavit de naviculariorum collegio adlegere, habiturus apostolum quandoque nauclerum Marcionem. Praestruximus quidem adversus Antitheses nihil proficere proposito Marcionis quam putat diversitatem Iegis et evangelii, ut et hanc a creatore dispositam, denique praedicatam in repromissione novae legis et novi sermonis et novi testamenti. Sed quoniam attentius argumentatur apud illum suum nescio quem ÏÏ Î½ÏÎ±Î»Î±á½·ÏÏÏÎ¿Î½, id est commiseronem, et ÏÏ Î¼Î¼Î¹ÏÎ¿á½»Î¼ÎµÎ½Î¿Î½, id est coodibilem, in leprosi purgationem, non pigebit ei occurrere et inprimis figuratae legis vim ostendere, quae in exemplo leprosi non contingendi, immo ab omni commercio submovendi, communicationem prohibebat hominis delictis commaculati, cum qualibus et apostolus cibum quoque vetat sumere;
passages.english: Finally, leaving their boats, they followed him, understanding that he was the very one who had begun to do what he had proclaimed. It is another matter if he wished to enrol [apostles] from the guild of boatmen, intending one day to have Marcion the shipmaster as an apostle. We have indeed already laid it down against the Antitheses that what Marcion takes to be a difference between the law and the gospel does nothing for his purpose, since this too was arranged by the creator, and indeed foretold in the promise of a new law and a new word and a new covenant. But since he argues rather carefully, with that fellow-sufferer of his, whoever he is, his *synpalaistros*, that is, 'co-wretch', and *symmisoumenos*, that is, 'co-hated one', concerning the cleansing of the leper, I will not be reluctant to meet him, and first of all to show the force of the figurative law, which, in the example of the leper who was not to be touched, indeed to be removed from all dealings, forbade association with a person stained by sins, with such as the apostle forbids even to take food;
passages.notes: The Greek words are mis-encoded; probably συνταλαίπωρον ('fellow-sufferer', glossed as 'commiseronem') and συμμισούμενον ('co-hated'). Marcion's nameless companion is unidentified. 'nauclerum' alludes to Marcion's being a shipowner.

passages.original: Quodsi et auctoritas divina et rerum natura et communis sapientia non admittunt insaniam haereticam, occasio est et hic interpellandi quam brevissime de substantia corporis adversus phantasmata Marcionis. Si natus ex homine est, ut filius hominis, corpus ex corpore est. Plane facilius invenias hominem natum cor non habere vel cerebrum, sicut ipsum Marcionem, quam corpus, ut Christum Marcionis. Atque adeo inspice cor Pontici aut cerebrum.
passages.english: But if divine authority, the nature of things and common wisdom do not admit the heretical madness, here too is an occasion to interject, as briefly as possible, about the substance of [Christ's] body, against Marcion's phantoms. If he was born of a human being, as son of man, he is body from body. Clearly you would more easily find a man born without a heart or a brain, like Marcion himself, than without a body, like Marcion's Christ. And so, examine the heart, or the brain, of the man from Pontus.

passages.original: Nam sicut sanis medicum nemo adhibet, ita nec in tantum extraneis, quantum est homo a deo Marcionis, suum habens et auctorem et protectorem, et ab illo potius medicum Christum. Hoc similitudo praeiudicat, ab eo magis praestari medicum ad quem pertinent qui languent. Unde autem et Ioannes venit in medium? Subito Christus, subito et Ioannes. Sic sunt omnia apud Marcionem, quae suum et plenum habent ordinem apud creatorem. Sed de Ioanne cetera alibi. Ad praesentes enim quosque articulos respondendum est. Nunc illud tuebor, ut demonstrem et loannem Christo et Christum loanni convenire, utique prophetae creatoris, qua Christum creatoris, atque ita erubescat haereticus, loannis ordinem frustra frustratus. Si enim nihil omnino administrasset Ioannes, secundum Esaiam vociferator in solitudinem et praeparator viarum dominicarum per denuntiationem et laudationem paenitentiae, si non etiam ipsum inter ceteros tinxisset, nemo discipulos Christi manducantes et bibentes ad formam discipulorum Ioannis assidue ieiunantium et orantium provocasset, quia, si qua diversitas staret inter Christum et Ioannem et gregem utriusque, nulla esset comparationis exactio, vacaret provocationis intentio.
passages.english: For as no one calls a doctor for the healthy, so neither for those so foreign as man is to Marcion's god, man having his own author and protector, and from him rather [having] Christ as doctor. The comparison prejudges this: that a doctor is rather provided by him to whom the sick belong. And where, too, did John spring from into the middle? Suddenly Christ, suddenly John too. So it is with everything in Marcion, which has its own complete order with the creator. But the rest about John elsewhere; for we must answer each point as it comes. Now I will maintain this, to show that John fits Christ and Christ John, John being of course a prophet of the creator, as Christ is the creator's, and so let the heretic blush, having frustrated the order of John in vain. For if John had administered nothing at all, as, according to Isaiah, the crier in the wilderness and the preparer of the Lord's ways by proclaiming and commending repentance, if he had not also dipped [Christ] himself among the rest, no one would have challenged Christ's disciples, who ate and drank, by the pattern of John's disciples, who constantly fasted and prayed; because, if there stood any difference between Christ and John and the flock of each, there would be no demand for comparison, the purpose of the challenge would be void.

passages.original: Denique, Dividetur, inquit, pater in filium et filius in patrem, et mater in filiam et filia in matrem, et nurus in socrum et socrus in nurum. Hoc proelium inter parentes si in ipsis verbis tuba cecinit prophetae, vereor ne Michaeas Christo Marcionis praedicarit. Et ideo hypocritas pronuntiabat, caeli quidem et terrae faciem probantes, tempus vero illud non dinoscentes, quo scilicet adimplens omnis quae super ipsos fuerunt praedicata nec aliter docens debuerat agnosci.
passages.english: Finally, he says: Father will be divided against son and son against father, and mother against daughter and daughter against mother, and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law and mother-in-law against daughter-in-law. If the trumpet of the prophet sounded this war among kin in these very words, I fear Micah preached for Marcion's Christ. And therefore he declared them hypocrites, who could test the face of the sky and the earth but did not discern that time in which, namely, he ought to have been recognised as fulfilling all that had been foretold about them, and teaching nothing otherwise.

passages.original: Aut si propterea panem corpus sibi finxit quia eorporis carebat veritate, ergo panem debuit tradere pre nobis. Faciebat ad vanitatem Marcionis, ut panis crucifigeretur. Cur autem panem corpus suum appellat, et non magis peponem, quem Marcion cordis loco habuit? Non intellegens, ve- terem fuisse istam figuram corporis Christi,dicentis per Hieremiam, Adversus me cogitaverunt cogitatum, dicentes, Venite coniciamus lignum in panem eius, scilicet crucem in corpus eius.
passages.english: Or if he feigned the bread to be his body because he lacked the reality of a body, then he should have handed over bread for us. It would suit Marcion's emptiness for bread to be crucified. But why does he call bread his body, and not rather a melon, which Marcion had in place of a heart? Not understanding that this was an ancient figure of Christ's body, who says through Jeremiah: They devised a device against me, saying, Come, let us cast wood into his bread, that is, the cross into his body.

passages.original: Sed iam nec mibi competit principes huius aevi virtutes et potestates interpretari creatoris, quia ignorantiam illis adscribit apostolus, Iesum autem et secundum nostrum evangelium diabolus quoque in temptatione cognovit, et secundum commune instrumentum spiritus nequam sciebat eum sanctum dei esse et Iesum vocari et in perditionem eorum venisse. Etiam parabola fortis illius armati, quem alius validior oppressit et vasa eius occupavit, si in creatoris accipitur apud Marcionem, iam nec ignorasse ultra potuit creator deum gloriae, dum ab eo opprimitur, nec in cruce eum figere adversus quem valere non potuit, et superest ut secundum me quidem credibile sit scientes virtutes et potestates creatoris deum gloriae Christum suum crucifixisse, qua desperatione et malitiae redundantia servi quoque scelestissimi dominos suos interficere non dubitant.
passages.english: But now it does not even fall to me to interpret the princes of this age as the powers and authorities of the creator, because the apostle ascribes ignorance to them, whereas Jesus, even according to our gospel, was recognised also by the devil in the temptation, and according to the common scripture an evil spirit knew that he was the holy one of God and was called Jesus and had come for their destruction. Also the parable of that strong armed man whom another, stronger, overpowered and seized his goods, if it is taken in Marcion's view as being about the creator, then the creator could no longer have been ignorant of the God of glory, while being overpowered by him, nor have fixed on the cross one against whom he could not prevail; and it remains that, in my view at least, it is credible that the powers and authorities of the creator knowingly crucified the God of glory, his Christ, out of that despair and overflow of malice by which even the most wicked slaves do not hesitate to kill their masters.

passages.original: Hunc ascensum si Christus nobis praeparavit, ille erit Christus de quo Amos: Qui ascensum suum aedificat in caelos, utique sibi et suis. Exinde a quo sperabo nunc, nisi a quo haec audivi? Quem spiritum prohibet extingui, et quas prophetias vetat nihil haberi? utique non creatoris spiritum, nec creatoris prophetias secundum Marcionem. Quae enim destruit, ipse iam extinxit et nihil fecit, nec potest prohibere quae nihil fecit. Ergo incumbit Marcioni exhibere hodie apud ecclesiam suam exinde spiritum dei sui qui non sit extinguendus, et prophetias que non sint nihil habendae.
passages.english: If Christ has prepared this ascent for us, he will be the Christ of whom Amos [speaks]: "He who builds his ascent into the heavens," surely for himself and for his own. Next, from whom shall I now hope, if not from him from whom I have heard these things? What Spirit does he forbid to be quenched, and what prophecies does he forbid to be held as nothing? Surely not the Creator's Spirit, nor the Creator's prophecies, according to Marcion. For what he destroys he has himself already quenched and made nothing, and he cannot forbid [the treating as nothing of] what he has made nothing. Therefore it falls to Marcion to produce today in his church, from that point on, the Spirit of his god, which is not to be quenched, and prophecies which are not to be held as nothing.
passages.notes: "que" read as "quae". The bracketed phrase in the penultimate sentence makes explicit the elliptical sense of "nec potest prohibere quae nihil fecit".

passages.original: Quis est autem homo delicti, filius perditionis, quem revelari prius oportet ante domini adventum, extollens se super omne quod deus dicitur et omnem religionem, consessurus in templo dei et deum se iactaturus? Secundum nos quidem antichristus, ut docent veteres ac novae prophetiae, ut Ioannes apostolus, qui iam antichristos dicit processisse in mundum praecursores antichristi spiritus, negantes Christum in carne venisse, et solventes Iesum, scilicet in deo creatore: secundum vero Marcionem nescio ne sit Christus creatoris. Nondum venit apud illum. Quisquis est autem ex duobus, quaero cur veniat in omni virtute et signis et ostentis mendacii? propterea, inquit, quod dilectionem veritatis non susce- perint, ut salvi essent, et propter hoc erit eis instinctum fallaciae, ut iudicentur omnes qui non crediderunt veritati, sed consenserunt iniquitati.
passages.english: But who is the man of sin, the son of perdition, who must first be revealed before the Lord's coming, exalting himself above everything that is called god and above all religion, who is to sit in the temple of God and boast himself to be god? According to us, indeed, [he is] the Antichrist, as the old and new prophecies teach, as does John the apostle, who says that antichrists have already gone out into the world as forerunners of the spirit of Antichrist, denying that Christ has come in the flesh and dissolving Jesus, that is, [dissolving him] in [relation to] God the Creator. But according to Marcion, I do not know whether he may not be the Creator's Christ, for in his view [that Christ] has not yet come. But whichever of the two he is, I ask why he comes "in all power and signs and lying wonders"? "Because," he says, "they did not receive the love of the truth, so that they might be saved; and for this reason there will be for them an impulse of deception, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity."
passages.notes: "solventes Iesum" ("dissolving Jesus") echoes a variant reading of 1 John 4:3; "in deo creatore" is compressed and its sense uncertain. "susce- perint" read as "susceperint".
